record_identity.title: Anthropic withheld Claude Mythos 5.1 from UK AISI pre-release evaluation

incident_identity.historical_event_name: 2026 Anthropic Mythos 5.1 UK AISI pre-release evaluation withholding
incident_identity.date_basis: The Financial Times reported on 9 September 2026 that Anthropic had not provided Claude Mythos 5.1 to the UK AI Security Institute for pre-release testing. Anthropic launched Mythos 5.1 on 1 September 2026. The exact date on which Anthropic decided not to provide pre-release access is not established in the reviewed public evidence; 9 September is therefore used as the public reporting anchor rather than an asserted decision date.

summary: The Financial Times reported that Anthropic did not provide Claude Mythos 5.1 to the United Kingdom's AI Security Institute for pre-release evaluation before the model's 1 September 2026 launch, describing the episode as the first time Anthropic had withheld its latest major model from AISI in this way. Anthropic describes Mythos 5.1 as its newest Mythos-class model with gains in cybersecurity and biology and said access at the time was limited to a small set of vetted United States organisations. AISI had previously evaluated Anthropic's Mythos Preview and documented substantial autonomous cyber capability. At a 13 October parliamentary hearing, Anthropic’s Lord Booth-Smith said AISI had been offered restricted access at release and chose not to use it, and had since received unrestricted access. The testimony did not establish that an evaluation had been completed.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The Financial Times reports that Anthropic withheld Claude Mythos 5.1 from UK AISI pre-release testing and that UK officials viewed the loss of access as a national-security and strategic concern. Anthropic's own Mythos page confirms that Mythos 5.1 launched on 1 September 2026, has gains in cybersecurity and biology, and was described at launch as available only to a small set of vetted US organisations. AISI's public evaluation of the earlier Mythos Preview establishes that AISI had previously tested Anthropic's frontier cyber model and found significant improvements in autonomous cyber capability, including completion of a multi-stage simulated network attack. Together, these sources establish a change in external pre-release access and the material safety-assurance context, while not establishing Anthropic's internal motive for the decision. The occurrence therefore records the loss of a previously available independent pre-release evaluation pathway for a high-capability frontier model; it does not establish that Mythos 5.1 is unsafe or that Anthropic breached any legal or contractual duty. The provider page reviewed earlier describes expanded verified access; that page alone does not establish whether AISI later received the model. The 12 October parliamentary answer to HL3641 discusses voluntary developer relationships and other model tests. It does not expressly answer whether AISI subsequently tested Mythos 5.1; later access arrangements do not restore the missed pre-release opportunity. The 13 October oral evidence provides a later, more specific account: restricted access was offered at release and declined, and unrestricted access was subsequently provided. This qualifies an absolute no-offer interpretation of the earlier reporting. The complete terms, restriction rationale and test outcome remain unpublished; the witness did not confirm US direction.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The occurrence is an institutional assurance and access-governance failure surface rather than evidence of model misconduct. Independent frontier-model evaluation depends on evaluators receiving timely access before deployment or restricted release. Where an external national safety institute that previously evaluated a provider's frontier models no longer receives pre-release access, the state's ability to independently characterize capability, validate safeguards and identify weaknesses before use is reduced. The governance issue is therefore the interruption of an established assurance pathway and the dependence of national safety oversight on provider-controlled and potentially geopolitically constrained model access. Loss of evaluator access remains relevant to oversight independence. The investigative-access candidate remains unresolved because the applicable mandate, access arrangement and possible justified withholding are unavailable. The class does not require compulsory legal authority merely because access is voluntary. The reported loss establishes neither institutional capture, unsafe deployment nor absence of every independent evaluation. The independent-evaluation policy and assessor-involvement assessments are Boundary. The decisive missing facts are the complete assessment policy and other independent or non-developer evaluations. Later parliamentary testimony distinguishes a restricted offer that AISI declined from subsequent unrestricted access. The original restriction still requires assessment against the applicable arrangement; later access is neither proof of justified withholding nor proof that pre-release assurance was adequate. The earlier harm assessment concerns the missed full pre-release workflow, not permanent exclusion.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: For CAM, the incident is relevant to sovereign assurance, cross-border AI governance and the difference between voluntary provider cooperation and durable independent oversight capability. A national safety institute cannot independently evaluate a frontier model it cannot access. The case therefore illustrates how frontier-model availability, export controls, provider policy and geopolitical relationships can become operational dependencies for public-sector safety assurance even without any proven defect in the model itself.
assessment_boundaries: This record does not conclude that Claude Mythos 5.1 is unsafe, inadequately safeguarded or responsible for any harmful deployment outcome.

The reviewed public evidence does not establish that Anthropic acted at the direction of the United States government or that US protectionism was the cause of the decision; those propositions are reported concerns and interpretations rather than established motive.
The record does not assert that Anthropic had a legal, contractual or regulatory duty to provide Mythos 5.1 to UK AISI before release.

The Financial Times characterisation that this was the first time Anthropic withheld its latest major model from AISI is preserved as source-attributed reporting rather than independently reconstructed historical fact.
The occurrence concerns loss of pre-release independent evaluation access; it does not establish that no post-release evaluation, information sharing or subsequent cooperation will occur.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: UK AISI's pre-release evaluation role materially engaged independent oversight of Mythos 5.1, but Anthropic did not provide unrestricted pre-release access. At a 13 October parliamentary hearing the provider representative said restricted access had been offered, AISI declined, and full access existed later; he said he was not privy to the US decision-making rationale. That testimony is attributed source evidence, not proof that a restricted offer was adequate for AISI's original mandate or that UK oversight was deliberately obstructed. The effective independence and review capacity available before launch remain bounded by undisclosed mandate and access terms.

boundary_adjudication.material_engagement: The parliamentary Q144–146 testimony establishes an offered restricted access route and AISI's decision not to use it; it does not establish unrestricted pre-release access, policy motives or effective test scope. Later full access cannot repair the original pre-release window, and unsupported accusations of intentional capture are not inferred.

boundary_adjudication.decisive_blocker: The contemporaneous AISI-specific access agreement, testing mandate and technically effective restricted access envelope are not established. The provider's restricted-offer account does not prove sufficient independent pre-release scrutiny.
boundary_adjudication.resolution_requirements: An AISI/government contemporaneous pre-release mandate, actual restricted-access test affordances and record of required evaluator tasks could resolve adequate oversight. Later access and unspecified US official reasoning are not substitutes for that evidence.
